author: BBC News
description:
A leading safety researcher at the AI developer Anthropic has warned he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger saidthe risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but the technology may develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out. But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.

Hubinger's intervention came  in response to comments from Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who has just quit Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI.  "Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote.  "These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."

Reeta Chakrabarti presents BBC
title: AI expert warns it may kill all humans within a decade | BBC News

Fighting between the US and Iran has escalated further, with the biggest back and forth strikes targeting shipping since the war started.

author: BBC News
description:
On Tuesday, the UK government announced sweeping sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and accused settlers of ‘ethnic cleansing.’ 
 
Soon after, 11 other countries, including Canada, France, Spain and Poland, announced a ban on goods imported from illegal settlements. 
 
In response, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said there would "without a doubt" be a reaction from the US, adding that the move could have a “huge economic impact on British businesses." 
 
What do the sanctions suggest about the US’s complex relationship with its western allies? 
 
The Global Story’s Asma Khalid speaks with BBC State Department correspondent Tom Bateman about the diplomatic consequences of US allies sanctioning the West Bank.

author: BBC News
description:
Images have shown passengers sleeping on airport floors as more than 300 flights were cancelled on Wednesday after Tuesday’s technical problem at air traffic control.
 
Some 1,750 flights were cancelled on Tuesday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium, with hundreds of thousands of passengers affected by the chaos.
 
Nats, the air traffic control provider, has apologised for the issue - the firm's boss Martin Rolfe says there will be an investigation.
 
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman says the government has confidence in Rolfe and they're expecting to see a report into the issue in a week's time.

author: BBC News
description:
Regularly drinking tea and coffee at very hot temperatures increases the risk of cancer of the food pipe or gullet, known as oesophageal cancer, UK research suggests. 
 
Researchers say the findings, from a study of nearly a million people, make this the largest to date to establish the link. 
 
In the study, people who had their drinks "very hot" had around a three times higher risk of the cancer than "warm" tea or coffee drinkers - although experts stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low.

author: BBC News
description:
The UK had to "call out" Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank before it was "too late" to save the two-state solution, the foreign secretary has said. 
 
Ed Milliband has announced the UK would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements in the illegally occupied West Bank. 

Israel has built around 160 settlements housing 700,000 people since then, despite all Israeli settlements in the West Bank being illegal under international law. Around 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
 
Israel has responded with four "counter-measures" against the UK - including the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem, which is expected to shut in the next 30 days.
